b: It’s the Thursday “ask the readers” question. A reader writes:

Your site’s readers span a wide range of jobs, many of which involve dealing with members of the public in some fashion. I’ve seen a lot of advice for how people should interact with someone in my job over the years, and I roll my eyes because some of it is actually likely to start someone off on completely the wrong foot and make the employee less inclined to help them with their situation.

For example: I teach large classes at my university. If a student has an issue with something — course policy, grading, etc. — they should talk to me on their own behalf, not say things like, “Everyone has a problem with this.” I take statements about many people having an issue seriously whether a group shows up together, or a bunch of people put their names on a document about a thing, or a bunch of people contact me separately about it. Someone claiming to be a spokesperson for a bunch of anonymous others is less likely to be taken seriously than someone talking about just themself.
I think it could be interesting having a thread where people provide what one thing they most wish people knew about what is actually effective when dealing with someone in their job.

Oooh, great suggestion. Readers, what’s one thing the public (or others in your company) should know about how to deal with the person in your job most effectively? We’ll define “effectively” here as “most likely to get them the outcome they want.”
